en: The Therāpadāna:
Pilindavaccha Chapter 1.
The Apadāna of the Elder Pilindavaccha
“In the city of Haṃsavatī,
I was a gatekeeper;
my wealth was unshakable and immeasurable.”
Accumulated by me in my home,
having gone into seclusion and sat down,
I gladdened my mind.
Seated in that excellent palace, I then reflected in this way.
1.1. The Manner of Reflection.
“Great wealth has been acquired,
my harem is flourishing;
even the king invited me.”
Ānanda is the lord of the earth.
And this Buddha has arisen,
the Sage who appears only rarely.
"Wealth exists for me;
I shall give a gift to the Teacher.
Thus spoke the prince Paduma.
The Victor gave the supreme gift:
an elephant-king, a couch,
and no small amount of a headrest.
I too shall give a gift to the Saṅgha,
the most excellent of assemblies—
a gift never before given by others.
"I shall be the first to perform it.
Having reflected in many ways upon the happy fruit that comes from sacrifice to whomsoever, I said:
I saw the gift of requisites that fulfills my intentions;
I shall give these requisites.
In the Saṅgha, the most excellent of assemblies;
having never before given to others,
may I be the first to do so.
1.2. Accomplishing the Basis for Giving:
Having approached the reed-worker, he had a parasol made at that very time.
I gathered together one hundred and seventy thousand [monks].
One hundred thousand pieces of cloth—
I assembled them on one side;
I assembled hundreds of thousands of bowls on one side.
I had razors, knives,
needles, and nail-clippers,
as well as umbrellas, placed beneath it.
Having had fashioned palm-leaf fans, peacock-feather fans,
and chowries appropriate for that occasion.
I had a water-strainer made, as well as oil-drops suitable for that purpose,
needle-cases, and shoulder-strap holders.
Furthermore, I had a waistband made,
as well as a well-crafted support,
both of which were appropriate for that purpose.
Having filled a vessel for use, or even a metal bowl, with medicine,
I placed beneath the umbrella:
vacā, usīra, laṭṭhikamadhu,
long pepper, and black pepper.
He filled the vessel with myrobalan and ginger;
there were sandals and shoes.
Furthermore, I had water-squeezers made,
as well as well-crafted walking sticks,
all appropriate for that occasion.
The medicinal ointment tube,
the probe, the Dhammakuttara,
and the key with its five colors.
One should sew [the cloth] at the key-holder,
at the yoke, at the smoke-pipe,
and also at the lamp-holder.
I had a water-pot and a casket made,
as well as a pair of tongs and a pair of pincers, all of which were suitable for those [relics].
Furthermore, he had a water-strainer and a medicine-tube made, both of which were appropriate for those purposes.
Having had thrones, stools, and couches made of the four types of wood appropriate for them, he provided them.
I placed beneath the umbrella a woolen cushion,
a cotton-down cushion,
and even a wooden stool-cushion.
And I had well-crafted ivory ornaments made,
along with honey and rice-powder suitable for them.
Kuruvinde madhusitthe, [I provided] with honey and rice-powder.
Oil for warming the hands,
a pair of sandals, a wooden board,
a needle, a bed, and a rug.
In the lodging, at the foot-wiping cloth,
on the bedstead’s frame,
and on the tooth-stick and the Āṭalī tree—
In the case of lead, ointment, and fragrant substances;
in the fire-drill, the fruit-seat,
the bowl-cover, and the water-pot;
A ladle for water,
powder, dye, and a vessel;
a broom and a water-pot.
Likewise the rain-cloak,
the sitting mat, the itch-covering cloth,
and then the inner robe.
The upper robe and the outer cloak,
nasal ointment for cleansing the face,
abundant sour gruel and salt.
Honey and a drink of curd;
incense, rice-powder, and a filter;
and a cloth for wiping the mouth.
"Whatever is to be given— whatever exists and is permissible for the Teacher—
all this having been gathered together,"
I approached Ānanda;
having approached, [I spoke to] the king,
the progenitor of the Great Sage.
Having saluted him with my head, I spoke these words:
1.3. The Request for Alms and Lodging.
Born and raised together,
with minds united as one,
sharing both happiness and suffering.
And both are followers.
There is mental suffering,
O Tāvadehya, which belongs to you, O Arindama.
“If you are able, O Kṣatriya, you should dispel that suffering.
Your suffering is my suffering.”
The minds of both are one;
know that it is finished,
if you accept my offering.
“Know this, O Great King:
my suffering is difficult to dispel.
Since you are capable, let out a roar!”
One boon is difficult for you to grant:
as much as there is in my realm,
and as long as I live;
If you have need of these,
I shall give them to you without hesitation.
Indeed, O Deva, you have roared.
That much boasting was in vain;
today I shall know you,
established in all dharmas.
“You have squeezed me too hard while I was giving you [alms];
what need have you for me being squeezed?”
"Tell me what you desire.
"O Great King, I desire the Supreme Buddha, the Unsurpassed One;"
"I shall feed the Perfectly Awakened One;
let not my life be in vain.
"I grant you another boon."
Do not entreat the Tathāgata;
the Buddha cannot be given away by anyone,
just like a radiant wish-fulfilling gem.
"Was it not you yourself, O King,
who thundered as far as your own life extends?
By giving up your life,"
"It is fitting to give to the Tathāgata.
"The Great Hero is beyond comparison;
the Victor cannot be surpassed by anyone."
“The Buddha has not granted my request;
grant me instead immeasurable wealth.
“Let us go before the judge.”
We shall ask for a definitive explanation;
they will speak according to the facts,
and we shall inquire further accordingly.
Taking the king by the hand,
I went before the judges to the court of justice.
I spoke these words:
“Listen to me, O dice-watchers;
the king has granted me a boon.”
Without setting anything aside,
even my life, I made the invitation.
To me, who had been granted that boon—
I have the most excellent Buddha as my superior;
the Buddha is my good fortune.
Cut through my doubt.
“We shall hear your words,
O protector of the earth, the king;
having heard the words of both, [we shall act].”
Let us cut through our doubt in this matter:
O King, everything that was seized by him has been given back to you by you.
"Without setting anything aside,
he even invited [me] to share his life.
Having fallen into hardship,"
I requested the unsurpassed boon;
knowing me to be deeply afflicted,
he granted me the power to grasp all.
“You have been defeated, O King;
the Tathāgata should be given [the victory].
The doubt of both has been severed.”
"Stay right where you are!
Having stood right there, the king spoke these words to Aṅkasa:
“Give it to me as well,
so that I too may obtain a Buddha again.
“Having fulfilled your intention,” [he said].
Having fed the Tathāgata,
you should then give [food] again to the Perfectly Enlightened One for the sake of the illustrious Ānanda.
1.4. The Discourse on the Invitation:
Having paid homage to the Arahants and also to the noble Ānanda;
Being satisfied and gladdened,
I approached the Fully Awakened One; having approached the Fully Awakened One, I—
Having bowed my head to him who has crossed the flood and is free from taints,
I spoke these words.
"O One with Vision, together with your hundred thousand seers, please accept [this];
gladdening my heart."
"Come to my dwelling. Thus spoke Padumuttara,
the Knower of the World,
the recipient of offerings.
Knowing my intention,
the Visionary One consented;
knowing his consent, [I rejoiced].
Having paid homage to the Teacher,
joyful and uplifted in heart,
I returned to my home.
1.5. Having gathered my friends and ministers for the distribution of gifts,
I spoke these words:
‘Just as a wish-fulfilling gem is very difficult for me to find,
by what means shall we honor it?’
Immeasurable and incomparable;
Incomparable, peerless, wise,
The Victor, without rival.
Likewise, he who is equal to the Unequalled,
the peerless Bull among Men— truly,
his service is difficult to perform.
"Bringing together various flowers, let us construct a flower pavilion worthy of the Buddhas."
"This will be a fitting offering for the Buddhas;
it shall be an offering surpassing all others.
Whether it be an *uppalā* or a *padumā*,...
Vassika, adhimuttaka,
campaka, and nāgapuppha—
these I had fashioned into a pavilion.
I prepared six thousand seats under the shade of the parasol;
the last seat was mine.
A hundred is worth more.
I provided a hundred thousand seats shaded by parasols.
Having prepared food and drink,
I announced the time.
When the time had been announced,
The Great Sage Padumuttara,
together with a hundred thousand masters,
came to my dwelling.
Holding a white parasol over a pavilion of full-blown flowers,
together with one hundred thousand masters (vasīs),...
The Supreme Person sat down.
"A hundred thousand parasols,
and a hundred thousand seats;"
"Accept what is allowable and blameless,
O Visionary One! said Padumuttara,
the Knower of the World.
The recipient of the oblations;
desiring to deliver me,
that Great Sage accepted them.
1.6. Discourse on Giving:
"I gave an alms-bowl individually to each and every bhikkhu."
They discarded the Sumbhaka bowl and used a copper bowl;
for seven days and nights, the Buddha [did so].
He sat in the flower-pavilion;
awakening many beings,
he set in motion the Wheel of Dhamma.
While setting in motion the Wheel of Dhamma beneath a flower pavilion for the eighty-four thousand [monks],
There was a realization of the Dhamma.
When the seventh day had arrived,
the Great Sage Padumuttara—
Seated in the shade of a palm tree, he spoke these verses.
1.7. The Exposition.
“I shall proclaim that excellent gift,
which the young brahmin gave to me,
which was without deficiency.”
Listen to me as I speak:
elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry—
the fourfold army.
They will always attend upon him;
this is the fruit of all-giving.
Elephants as vehicles, horses as vehicles—
A palanquin and a chariot;
these shall constantly attend upon me—
this is the fruit of all my giving.
Sixty thousand chariots,
adorned with every ornament,
shall constantly attend upon him.
This is the fruit of all-giving:
sixty thousand musical instruments and well-adorned drums.
They shall always proclaim this:
such is the fruit of all giving.
Eighty-six thousand—
Women were beautifully adorned,
wearing variegated garments and ornaments, with jewels and earrings fastened upon them.
With arched brows and beautiful eyes,
well-proportioned and slender-waisted,
they shall always attend upon him.
This is the fruit of all giving:
for thirty thousand eons,
he will delight in the world of the gods.
A thousand times he will exercise divine sovereignty as Lord of the Gods;
a thousand times he will be a king.
He will become a wheel-turning monarch;
his regional sovereignty will be vast and beyond counting.
For one who dwells in the world of the gods,
endowed with meritorious deeds,
the limit of that world of the gods—
He will hold up a jeweled parasol.
Whenever he desires shade,
there shall be a covering made of cloth and flowers.
Knowing his mind,
he will provide constant protection;
having passed away from the world of the gods, he will come here.
Urged on by the root of the wholesome,
and endowed with meritorious deeds,
he will become a kinsman of Brahmā.
In a hundred thousand aeons,
one born of the Okkāka clan,
known by the family name Gotama, will appear.
“The Teacher shall appear in the world.
Having directly known all this,
Gotama, the bull of the Sakyans;
Sitting within the community of bhikkhus,
he will place him in the foremost position among those named Pilindavaccha.
He becomes a disciple of the Teacher,
honored by the devas, the asuras, and the gandhabbas.
Having become dear to all— the bhikkhus, the bhikkhunīs, and likewise to the householders—
He will dwell free from taints.
1.8. Discourse on the Benefits of Giving:
An action performed during a hundred thousand [aeons]—
It showed me its fruit right here;
like an arrow released from a bow,
it has incinerated my defilements.
"Aho! Well-performed is my deed in this unsurpassed field of merit,
having performed service where— "
I have attained the unshakable state.
For that young man who gave the supreme gift without deficiency—
He was the first to go before;
this is the fruit of that gift.
1.8.1. The Six Benefits of the Parasol.
Having given a mat to the Sugata and to the Saṅgha, the most excellent of assemblies,
I enjoy eight benefits.
It is suitable for my work.
I know neither cold nor heat,
and dust and dirt do not cling to me.
May I be free from calamity and free from misfortune,
and may I always be held in high esteem.
May I have delicate skin.
My mind became clear as I wandered through existence for six hundred thousand births.
Adorned with every ornament,
by the power of that karma,
except for this present birth.
They carry it over my head.
Why is it that in this birth there is no holding of a parasol for me?
All my work has been done for the sake of the parasol and the bowl of liberation.
1.8.2. The Benefits of the Robe-Cloth.
Having given robes to the Sugata and to the Saṅgha,
the most excellent of assemblies,
I enjoy eight benefits.
Worthy of my labor.
Golden-hued, stainless,
radiant, and majestic;
My body becomes supple as I wander through existence;
hundreds of thousands of robes [are worn].
White, yellow, and red—
these they wear upon my head;
this is the fruit of the gift of cloth.
Silken garments, woolen blankets,
and those made of linen and cotton—
I obtain them in every respect.
From that result, I [arose].
1.8.3. The Benefits:
Having given alms-bowls to the Sugata, [one attains these benefits].
In the Saṅgha, the most excellent of assemblies,
I experience ten benefits that are appropriate for my actions.
In a golden bowl, in a jeweled bowl,
and even in a silver bowl;
in a bowl made of ruby—
I always enjoy [these things];
free from calamity and free from misfortune,
I am always honored.
I obtain food, drink,
clothing, and bedding;
my wealth does not perish.
I am one whose mind is established;
I am always a lover of the Dhamma,
with few defilements and free from taints.
Whether in the world of the gods or among humans,
these qualities follow one,
just as a shadow follows a tree.
They do not abandon me in any circumstance.
1.8.4. The Advantage of the Axe:
Bound by the fetters of the mind,
Many well-fashioned adzes were given by me to the Best of Buddhas and likewise to the Saṅgha.
I experience eight benefits appropriate to my deeds:
I am brave and far-reaching.
I have reached perfection in the grounds of self-confidence.
I am possessed of fortitude and energy,
with my mind always exerted.
I obtain everywhere the knowledge that cuts off defilements— subtle, incomparable, and pure.
As the result of that, I am [thus].
1.8.5. The Benefits of the Sword:
Without harshness, without cruelty...
Having given many books written in ink,
with a mind full of serene confidence,
to the Buddha and likewise to the Saṅgha.
I experience these five benefits,
which are appropriate for my deeds:
a virtuous friend and energy.
Patience and the weapon of loving-kindness;
because the arrow of craving has been severed,
there is the unsurpassed weapon of wisdom.
Their knowledge is equal to a vajra;
it is from that very source that I have obtained this.
1.8.6. The Benefits of the Needle.
Having given needles to the Sugata and to the Saṅgha,
the most excellent of assemblies,
I enjoy five benefits.
It is suitable for my deeds.
There is no doubt; it cuts away uncertainty;
he is handsome and possesses wealth.
Possessing sharp wisdom, I have always been so while wandering through various states of existence.
Even in matters that are profound and subtle, I am wise.
I saw the goal with knowledge;
that knowledge of mine, like the point of a diamond, is a non-slaying.
1.8.7. The Benefits of Nail-Cutting:
Having given nail-cutters to the Sugata and to the Saṅgha, the supreme assembly;
I experience these five benefits,
which are appropriate for my deeds:
female and male slaves, cattle, and horses.
In many dramas, I receive food as a hired servant;
whether as a washerman, a cook,
or in any other capacity, I obtain it everywhere.
1.8.8. The Benefits of Offering a Fan and a Beautiful Palmyra-Fan:
Having given a fan and a beautiful palmyra-fan to the Sugata, [one gains great merit].
I experience eight benefits that are appropriate for my deeds;
I know neither cold nor heat.
No fever exists;
I know no distress that would torment my mind.
The fire of lust, the fire of hatred and delusion,
the fire of conceit, and the fire of views—
all these fires have been extinguished within me.
From that [merit] of mine, as a result:
1.8.9. Peacock-feather Whisks and Chauris Peacock-feather whisks and chauris,
Having given to the Sangha, the supreme assembly;
with my defilements stilled,
I dwell free from blemish.
1.8.10. The Water Strainer and Dhamma-Vessel:
Having given a water strainer and an excellent Dhamma-vessel to the Sugata, [one gains great merit].
I experience five benefits that are appropriate for my deeds,
having transcended all [others].
I obtain divine life;
I am always difficult for thieves or enemies to overcome.
One does not cause harm even with a weapon or poison;
there is no untimely death for such a one.
This is the outflow for me from those [deeds].
1.8.11. The Benefits of the Oil Stream:
Having given an oil stream to the Sugata,
In the Saṅgha, the most excellent of assemblies,
I experience five benefits that are appropriate to my deeds.
Of beautiful form and auspicious,
with a mind well-uplifted,
may I be undistracted in mind.
Protected by all safeguards.
1.8.12. The Benefits of Giving a Needle Case:
Having given a needle case to the Sugata,
In the Saṅgha, the most excellent of assemblies,
I experience three benefits that are appropriate for my actions.
Mental happiness, physical happiness,
and the happiness born of the postures—
may I obtain these qualities.
As a result of that, I [attained this].
1.8.13. The Benefits of the Shoulder-Yoke:
Having given shoulder-yokes to the Victor,
In the Saṅgha, the most excellent of assemblies,
I experience three benefits that are appropriate for my deeds.
I find a firm footing in the true Dhamma;
I remember my second existence;
everywhere I possess beautiful skin.
As a result of that, I [attained this].
1.8.14. The Benefits of the Girdle:
Having given a girdle to the Victor,
In the Saṅgha, the most excellent of assemblies,
I experience the five benefits appropriate to my deeds.
I am unshakable in the meditative absorptions;
I have mastery over the absorptions;
I am one whose assembly is indivisible.
My words are always authoritative.
I am possessed of established mindfulness;
no fear exists within me.
Whether in the world of the gods or among humans, these qualities follow one after another.
1.8.15. The Benefits of the Support.
Having given a bowl to the Jina and to the Saṅgha,
the most excellent assembly,
the heir [of the Buddha] with five-colored [robes].
I am immovable by anything whatsoever.
Whatever teachings have been heard by me,
they awaken mindfulness and wisdom.
They do not perish for me;
they become well-determined. 1.8.16.
The Advantage of Being a Vessel.
Having given a vessel and articles for use to the Buddha, the supreme among assemblies,
I experience three benefits.
Suitable for my work—
made of gold, made of jewels,
and even made of crystal.
I obtain vessels made of ruby, as well as a wife,
male servants, and female servants.
Elephants, chariots, and infantry;
a wife who is devoted to her husband,
and all kinds of enjoyments at all times.
I have mastered all branches of knowledge,
including the words of mantras, various traditional scriptures, and many diverse crafts.
...enjoyments at all times.
1.8.17. The Benefits of a Bowl:
Having given a bowl to the Sugata,
In the Saṅgha, the most excellent of assemblies,
I experience three benefits that are appropriate for my actions.
Made of gold, made of jewels,
and likewise made of crystal;
and indeed made of ruby.
I receive [alms] in a shallow bowl made of wood, one made of fruit,
and also in a lotus leaf.
And in the vessel for drinking honey-wine,
I obtain a bowl;
in the practice of virtue, I am established in right conduct.
And in the performance of proper conduct;
these qualities I have obtained as the result thereof.
1.8.18. The Benefits of Medicine Having given medicine to the Sugata and to the Saṅgha,
the most excellent of assemblies,
I experience the ten benefits that are appropriate for my deeds:
long-lived, strong, and wise.
Possessing beauty, fame, and happiness;
free from misfortune and calamity,
may I always be honored.
There is no separation from what is dear to me, owing to that merit of his which flowed to me.
1.8.19. The Benefits of Sandals.
Having given a pair of sandals to the Saṅgha,
the most excellent of assemblies,
I enjoy three benefits.
Suitable for my deeds:
elephant-vehicles, horse-vehicles,
palanquins, and chariots.
Sixty million [beings] always attend upon me—
those made of jewels and those made of copper.
Golden and silver sandals arise for me as I wander through existence, at every step I take.
They run toward the certainty [of the path],
purifying their past conduct;
may they obtain these virtues.
As a result of that, I [attained this].
1.8.20. The Benefits of Sandals:
Having given sandals to the Sugata,
In the Saṅgha, the most excellent of assemblies;
having mounted the sandals of psychic power,
I dwell wherever I desire.
1.8.21. The Benefits of Giving a Water-Wringer:
Having given a water-wringing cloth to the Buddha, the supreme among assemblies;
I experience five benefits,
appropriate for my deeds:
I am golden-hued and free from dust.
Radiant and majestic;
my limbs are supple,
and dust and dirt do not adhere to them.
I have obtained these qualities as the result of that [merit].
1.8.22. The Benefits of the Carrying Staff.
Having given a walking staff to the Sugata and to the Sangha, the supreme assembly,
I enjoy these six benefits.
It is appropriate for my work.
My sons are many,
and no fear exists within me.
I am always easy to support and protected by all safeguards;
I do not even know of any lapse.
My mind is untroubled.
1.8.23. The Benefits of Medicinal Herbs and Eye Salve:
Having given medicinal herbs and eye salve...
In the Buddha and the Sangha, the supreme assembly,
I experience eight benefits appropriate to my deeds.
I have wide eyes, white,
yellow, and red; my gaze is clear and serene.
Free from all diseases,
I obtain the divine eye and the unsurpassed eye of wisdom.
I have obtained these qualities as the result of that [deed].
1.8.24. The Benefits of the Key.
Having given the key to the Sugata,
to the Saṅgha, the most excellent of assemblies,
[he performed] the opening of the door of the Dhamma.
I obtain the key of knowledge.
1.8.25. The Benefits of Giving Keys:
Having given keys in the house, [one gains these fruits].
In the Buddha and the Sangha, the supreme assembly,
I experience these two benefits,
which are appropriate for my past deeds.
With little anger and free from distress, I wandered through the realms of existence.
1.8.26. The Advantage of Exertion.
Having given what was appropriate to the Sugata and to the Saṅgha,
the most excellent of assemblies, I enjoy five benefits.
Suitable for my work.
I do not waver in meditative absorptions;
I am a master of meditative absorptions.
May I have an unbreakable assembly and my words always be respected;
may the perfection of wealth arise for me.
As I wander through existence.
1.8.27. The Benefits of the Smoke-Eye:
Having given the smoke-eye to the Conqueror, [one attains these benefits].
In the Saṅgha, the most excellent of assemblies,
I experience three benefits that are appropriate for my deeds.
My mindfulness is upright,
and my tendons are well-knit;
I obtain the divine eye.
It was through the result of that [merit] that I [became so].
1.8.28. The Benefits of Offering Lamps:
Having given lamps to the Conqueror, the bearer of light...
In the Saṅgha, the most excellent of assemblies,
I experience three benefits that are appropriate for my deeds.
One who is well-born, endowed with the [right] factors, wise, and esteemed by the Buddhas—
may he obtain these virtues.
As a result of that, I [attained this].
1.8.29. Tumbaka-karaṇḍa:
In a gourd and in a basket,
Having given to the Buddha, the supreme among assemblies,
I experience ten benefits that are appropriate to my own deeds.
Sugutta is endowed with happiness,
the Tathāgata of great renown;
free from misfortune, he is delicate.
Avoiding all that is called "evil," I have attained vast virtues;
even my very movement is equal [to theirs].
Having well avoided the aversion toward gourds and baskets,
I obtain the four castes.
And the tusks of elephants;
these do not perish for me—
this is the fruit of the gift of gourds.
1.8.30. The Benefits of Giving Purifiers:
Having given purifiers to the Buddha and the Saṅgha, the supreme assembly, one attains these benefits.
I experience five benefits,
which are appropriate for my deeds;
I am endowed with all the auspicious marks.
Endowed with longevity and wisdom,
and liberated from all weariness,
my body remains so at all times.
1.8.31. The Benefits of Pippala Fruits:
Having given pippala fruits to the Saṅgha with well-sharpened, thin-edged [knives], one obtains these benefits.
I obtain incomparable and pure knowledge that destroys the defilements.
1.8.32. The Benefits of the Tongs.
Having given a pair of sandals to the Sugata and to the Saṅgha,
the most excellent of assemblies,
may there arise the knowledge that shatters the defilements.
I obtain incomparable purity.
Having given a nose-salve to the Sugata, there is this benefit in the nose-salve.
In the Saṅgha, the most excellent of assemblies,
I experience eight benefits that are appropriate for my deeds.
Faith, virtue, and also moral shame,
as well as the quality of moral dread;
learning, generosity, and patience—
Wisdom is my eighth quality.
Having given a seat to the Sugata, [one gains these benefits].
In the Saṅgha, the most excellent of assemblies,
I experience the five benefits appropriate to my own actions.
I am born into a high family,
I become one of great wealth;
everyone pays me honor.
My fame has spread far and wide.
For a hundred thousand eons,
there were four-cornered couches.
They constantly attend upon me;
I am one who delights in sharing.
1.8.35. The Benefits of the Bedding Seat.
Having given mats to the Sugata and to the Saṅgha,
the most excellent of assemblies,
I enjoy these six benefits.
Worthy of my deeds. With limbs symmetrical and well-proportioned,
soft and beautiful to behold;
I obtain the retinue of wisdom;
this is the fruit of the gift of a lotus.
[I also obtain] mattresses and pillows.
Many painters will paint for me;
I shall receive various fine cloths, rugs, and blankets.
I receive cotton cloths from weavers,
soft deerskins, and woven bands,
as well as various kinds of rugs.
This is the fruit of giving medicine.
As far back as I can remember myself,
from the time I attained the age of discretion;
I am not empty; I possess the essence of meditation—this is the fruit of the gift of a pillow.
1.8.36. The Benefits of a Pillow.
Having given a seat-cushion to the Victor and to the Saṅgha,
the most excellent of assemblies,
I enjoy the six benefits.
Suitable for my work:
wool, lotus fibers,
and red sandalwood.
I always offer my head as an ornament upon the excellent Eightfold Path.
Regarding the four fruits of recluseship:
having generated knowledge regarding them,
may you dwell at all times.
In generosity, self-control, and restraint,
and in the immeasurables and the form-spheres;
having generated knowledge regarding these,
One should dwell [thus] at all times.
Regarding the duties, virtues, practice,
and the performance of proper conduct;
Having generated knowledge regarding them,
may I dwell at all times,
whether on the walking-path or in the place of striving.
Regarding energy as a factor of enlightenment:
having generated knowledge in these,
I dwell according to my wish.
Virtue, concentration, wisdom,
and supreme liberation—
having generated knowledge regarding these, [one should practice].
I dwell in happiness.
Having given a fruit-seat to the Victor, [one dwells in happiness]. 1.8.37. The Benefits of the Fruit-Seat.
Having given a fruit-seat to the Conqueror, [one dwells in happiness].
In the Saṅgha, the most excellent of assemblies,
I experience these two benefits,
which are appropriate for my deeds.
I find many excellent couches made of gold, of jewels, and of ivory.
This is the fruit of the fruit-seat.
1.8.38. The Benefits of the Footstool:
Having given a footstool to the Victor, [one receives these benefits].
In the Saṅgha, the most excellent of assemblies,
I experience these two benefits,
which are appropriate for my past deeds.
I obtain many vehicles;
this is the fruit of the footstool.
Servants, maidservants, and wives—
And those other dependents who attend upon me properly—
this is the fruit of the footstool.
1.8.39. The Benefits of Offering Oil for Anointing:
Having given oil for anointing to the Saṅgha, the most excellent of assemblies;
I experience these five benefits,
which are appropriate for my deeds:
being free from illness and possessed of beauty.
Quickness in grasping the Dhamma,
And the obtaining of food and drink—
these five qualities, including long life, are mine.
1.8.40. The Benefits of Ghee-Oil:
Having given ghee-oil to the Saṅgha, the most excellent of assemblies;
I experience five benefits that are appropriate for my deeds:
I am steadfast and endowed with beauty.
With limbs always joyful and free from disease, I am devoid of poison;
this is the fruit of ghee and oil.
1.8.41. The Benefits of Giving Face-Cleansing Mitts:
Having given a face-cleansing mitt to the Buddha and the Saṅgha, the supreme assembly;
I experience these five benefits,
which are appropriate for my deeds:
my throat is purified and my voice is sweet.
Free from cough and phlegm,
the fragrance of blue lotuses constantly wafts from my mouth.
1.8.42. The Praise of Curd:
Having given excellent curd to the Buddha and the Saṅgha, the supreme assembly;
I eat the food of the Deathless;
mindfulness directed to the body is superior.
1.8.43. The Benefits of Honey.
Having given honey endowed with color, fragrance, and flavor to the Conqueror and his assembly,
[one gains] that which is incomparable and immeasurable.
May I drink the essence of liberation.
Having given the flavor as it truly is, [I shall experience] the benefit of that flavor.
In the Buddha and the Sangha, the supreme assembly,
I experience the four fruits;
may these be in accordance with my past deeds.
1.8.45. The Benefits of Food and Drink:
Having given food and drink to the Buddha and the Saṅgha, the supreme assembly;
I experience the ten benefits appropriate to my deeds:
long-lived, strong, and wise.
He is handsome, famous, and happy;
he is always a winner of food and drink,
heroic, and possessed of wisdom.
May I obtain these virtues while wandering through the cycle of existence.
1.8.46. The Benefits of Incense.
Having offered incense to the Sugata and to the Saṅgha,
the most excellent of assemblies,
I experience ten benefits.
It is appropriate for my deeds:
fragrant-bodied, illustrious,
quick-witted, and renowned.
One of sharp wisdom, vast wisdom,
possessing laughter and profound wisdom;
one of expansive and swift wisdom.
Wandering through various states of existence,
it is now, by the power of that very [practice],
that he has attained the auspicious bliss of peace.
1.9. Common Benefits:
My defilements have been incinerated;
all states of existence have been uprooted.
Like a snake that has severed its bonds,
I dwell free from taints.
Welcome indeed has come to me!
In the presence of my Buddha,
the three knowledges have been attained;
the teaching of the Buddha has been fulfilled.
The four analytical knowledges,
these eight liberations,
and the six direct knowledges have been realized.
“Thus was the teaching of the Buddha spoken.
In this way, it is said, the venerable elder Pilindavaccha recited these verses.
This is the first legend of the elder Pilindavaccha.
